posts.reason: A first-person method for finding problems worth solving, grounded in one detailed worked example, with a thread full of first-hand accounts of how much autonomy engineers really have.
A long argument backed by several small experiments with real numbers, candid about how rough they are, on what cheap agent labour changes about performance work.

A decision framework that walks from the simplest retrieval option to the most complex with rough cost and latency arithmetic, and a thread of practitioners who mostly agree and name the cases where it breaks.
A design wish list with concrete proposed syntax, including sum types with pattern matching and polymorphic foreign keys, and a thread pointing to prior art.
An argued essay on what anger at work actually costs the angry person, with a carefully hedged exception for 'professional anger'.
Three realisations from the author's forties: distrust your own narratives, doubt single causes, and treat emotions as information.
A clear plain-language explainer of the parts of an agent harness, with a worked example and a thread of practitioners comparing notes.
Careful reverse engineering, with decompiled call paths and live server responses, showing that locally generated images still carry a server-issued identifier.
A working novelist's case for reading as the writer's real training, and a thread full of prose-style recommendations.
Real news clippings set beside Ballard and Gibson, and a long literary thread on what the cyberpunk writers got right and wrong.
A long short story, told as a memoir, about prediction markets and AI bots taking over a life; many readers took it for true.
